metadata.description: Scenario-Based Study Guide for AZ-204 certification - validates skills for designing, building, testing, deploying, and maintaining cloud-native applications on Microsoft Azure.

questions.title: Container Deployment Choice
questions.scenario: You need to deploy a new containerized web application on Azure. The app consists of a single container running a stateless web service. The team is small and has limited Kubernetes expertise. They require a quick deployment with minimal management overhead, but the solution must still scale to handle increasing traffic.
questions.questionText: Given a choice between running the container on Azure App Service (Web App for Containers) or on a fully managed Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster, which should you choose?

choices.text: Azure App Service (Web App for Containers)

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about team expertise and operational overhead. Which option lets a small team ship a single container fastest with the least management?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Choose Azure App Service's Web App for Containers for this single-container scenario. App Service lets you deploy the container in a PaaS environment with minimal management overhead - you don't need to run or maintain any Kubernetes control plane. AKS would be overkill since no multi-container orchestration or custom Kubernetes features are needed. Web App for Containers allows the team to focus on the app, not infrastructure.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure App Service for Containers gives you a dedicated container hosting environment with support for deployment slots, auto-scaling, and easy SSL/TLS integration.
  • It abstracts the entire cluster, so there's no Kubernetes API exposure or control - which is fine for a single container app.
  • This choice trades off some low-level control for simplicity: AKS would allow more complex scenarios but introduces operational complexity.

questions.title: Choosing a Compute Service for a Web App
questions.scenario: A company is migrating a monolithic ASP.NET web application from on-premises to Azure. The app will serve HTTP requests and has stateful sessions managed in-memory. They want to minimize infrastructure management.
questions.questionText: Should they deploy the application to Azure App Service or break it into Azure Functions?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider the application's architecture — monolithic, stateful, and HTTP-based. Which compute model fits that shape without major refactoring?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use Azure App Service (Web App) for this migration. App Service is designed to host web applications (including ASP.NET apps) with minimal modification - you can lift-and-shift the entire app into a managed web environment. Azure Functions is a Functions-as-a-Service model meant for discrete, stateless units of code that run on triggers - converting a monolithic web app into functions would require significant refactoring.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure App Service provides features like auto-scaling, staging slots, and integrated logging that support the monolithic app in production.
  • App Service can run in a stateful mode if the app uses session affinity or external session storage like Azure Cache for Redis.
  • By choosing App Service, you avoid the cold start and timeout limitations that a consumption-plan Function might impose.

questions.title: Serverless Workflow Orchestration
questions.scenario: You are implementing an order processing workflow composed of multiple steps: receive order, charge payment, update inventory, and send confirmation. Each step is implemented as a separate function. You need each step to execute in sequence with state maintained between steps.
questions.questionText: Which Azure service or pattern should you use to orchestrate these serverless functions?

choices.text: Azure Service Bus with manual orchestration
Standard Azure Functions with queue triggers

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The key requirement is maintaining state between sequential serverless steps. Which Azure pattern extends Functions to support stateful orchestration?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Leverage Azure Durable Functions, which enables stateful orchestration on top of Azure Functions. With Durable Functions, you can define an orchestrator function that calls each step (activity functions) in sequence, ensuring the workflow follows the required order. The platform automatically checkpoints progress to durable storage, so if a step fails or the process restarts, it can resume from the last checkpoint.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Durable Functions use an event-sourcing approach: the orchestrator function's progress is snapshotted to Azure Storage, and it replays the function to rebuild state when new events arrive.
  • The workflow can wait for human interaction or a timer using Durable function's waiting mechanics without consuming resources.
  • Durable Functions guarantee at-least-once execution for each activity - design idempotent activities or use built-in retry policies.

questions.title: Globally Distributed Data Store
questions.scenario: An online game needs to store player profile data. Requirements are low latency reads and writes for players around the world, automatic scaling to handle spikes, and flexible schema as profiles may evolve over time.
questions.questionText: Which backend should they choose for this scenario - Azure SQL Database or Azure Cosmos DB?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Focus on the three requirements together: global low-latency, elastic scaling, and flexible schema. Which data store is built around all three?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use Azure Cosmos DB for storing player profiles. Cosmos DB is designed for low latency and high throughput on a global scale. You can replicate data to multiple regions so players' reads/writes go to their nearest region. It supports multi-region writes, automatic scaling of throughput, and schema-less (NoSQL) nature allows evolving profile data without rigid schemas.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cosmos DB offers multi-master replication with conflict resolution, meaning writes can occur in any region.
  • Performance is priced in Request Units (RUs) allowing elastic throughput scaling - use autoscale mode to handle sudden surges.
  • Choose a consistency level (perhaps Session consistency) for each player session to ensure a player's own writes are immediately visible to them.

questions.title: Event-Driven Data Processing
questions.scenario: A retail application uses an Azure Cosmos DB container to store orders. They want to automatically trigger downstream processing whenever a new order is added, without constantly polling the database.
questions.questionText: What Azure feature can enable this reactive pattern?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about a built-in feature of Cosmos DB that streams mutations as they happen — no polling required.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use Azure Cosmos DB's Change Feed to react to new orders. The change feed lists all changes (inserts and updates) to documents in the order they occur. By using an Azure Function with a Cosmos DB Trigger bound to the change feed, each new order document will automatically invoke the function shortly after it's written.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The Cosmos DB change feed ensures ordering within a partition key, so changes for a given partition come out in sequence.
  • It's effectively an append-only log of changes - you can attach multiple independent consumers for different purposes.
  • The change feed provides at-least-once delivery semantics - duplicates are possible; design idempotent handlers.

questions.title: Secure Client File Uploads
questions.scenario: You are developing a web application where users can upload images and documents stored in Azure Blob Storage. For security, the application server should not expose storage account keys or handle file data directly.
questions.questionText: What is a secure way to allow clients to upload and download files using Azure Blob Storage?

choices.text: Proxy all uploads through the web server
Share storage account keys with clients

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can you grant time-limited, scoped access to a specific blob without exposing account keys or routing data through your server?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The secure pattern is to use Azure Blob Storage SAS tokens to delegate limited access to clients. The application creates a Shared Access Signature URL for the specific blob or container. This SAS token grants time-bound and permission-bound access. The client can then PUT the file to Blob Storage directly using this URL without needing account keys.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use User Delegation SAS when possible - this leverages Azure AD credentials to create the SAS, removing the need to use the storage account key at all.
  • Enforce HTTPS on SAS URLs and keep their lifetime short to reduce risk.
  • SAS aligns with least privilege principle: each SAS grants exactly the access needed and nothing more.

questions.title: Message Queue for Order Processing
questions.scenario: An e-commerce platform needs to decouple order submission from order fulfillment. Requirements include guaranteed at-least-once delivery, ability to detect and avoid duplicate order messages, and processing in roughly the order received.
questions.questionText: Should you use Azure Service Bus queues or Azure Storage queues for this scenario?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The scenario demands FIFO ordering and duplicate detection. Which Azure messaging tier offers those enterprise-grade broker features?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use Azure Service Bus Queues for the order messages. Service Bus is designed for enterprise messaging scenarios that require guaranteed delivery, ordering, and near exactly-once broker-side handling. It has built-in duplicate detection and supports ordered delivery using sessions. Azure Storage Queue is simpler but doesn't guarantee FIFO order and has no built-in duplicate detection.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure Service Bus queues support AMQP protocol, enabling features like long polling and push-style delivery to listeners.
  • With Sessions, you can achieve FIFO by grouping related messages - use session IDs to segregate and preserve sequence.
  • Duplicate detection (when enabled with message ID) can transparently ignore duplicate copies within a dedup window.

questions.title: Telemetry Ingestion at Scale
questions.scenario: A smart sensor network sends telemetry data from 100,000+ devices concurrently. The data needs to be ingested by a cloud gateway and processed in near real-time for anomalies.
questions.questionText: Which Azure service is best suited to ingest a high volume of events per second - Azure Event Hubs or Azure Event Grid?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: With 100K+ concurrent devices, you need a service designed for massive throughput streaming, not discrete event routing. Which Azure service is built for that scale?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use Azure Event Hubs for ingesting the sensor telemetry. Event Hubs is a big data streaming platform that can intake huge volumes of events and is designed for high-throughput, sequential event processing. It supports batching, temporal buffering, and the ability to replay or catch up on streams. Azure Event Grid is optimized for reactive discrete events, not continuous telemetry streams.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Event Hubs uses partitions - partition by device ID so processing can be parallelized but also logically grouped for order.
  • Event Hubs supports capture to Azure Blob Storage or Data Lake for automatic archival.
  • It supports both AMQP and Kafka protocols, so existing Kafka-based producers/consumers can talk to Event Hubs with minimal changes.

questions.title: Reactive Notifications for Blob Events
questions.scenario: A media processing workflow stores raw videos in Blob Storage. Whenever a new video blob is uploaded to a specific container, the system should automatically trigger an Azure Function to start encoding.
questions.questionText: What Azure service or mechanism should you use to react to the blob upload event?

choices.text: Azure Event Grid with Blob Storage events

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: You want push-based, near-instant reaction to a blob creation — not polling. Which Azure eventing service integrates natively with Blob Storage for this?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Set up Azure Event Grid on the Blob Storage account for blob creation events. Azure Blob Storage is natively integrated with Event Grid - when a new blob is uploaded, Event Grid generates a BlobCreated event. You can subscribe an Azure Function to those events. This is completely serverless, push-based, and reacts quickly (usually within seconds).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Event Grid guarantees at-least-once delivery of events and can use advanced filters to only trigger for relevant events.
  • The Blob Storage to Event Grid integration is much more immediate than legacy blob triggers which use polling.
  • You can chain events - Blob Created -> Event Grid -> Service Bus or Logic App if the process needs orchestration.

questions.title: Securing Application Secrets
questions.scenario: You are developing an Azure App Service web application that needs to connect to an Azure SQL Database and a third-party API. These require sensitive credentials. You want to avoid storing secrets in config files or code.
questions.questionText: How should the application securely store and access these secrets in Azure?

choices.text: Store secrets in Azure Key Vault
Store secrets in Azure Blob Storage

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about a centralized, access-controlled vault purpose-built for storing secrets, keys, and certificates in Azure.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use Azure Key Vault to store all sensitive credentials. Key Vault is a secure, central repository for keys/secrets/certificates. Configure your Azure App Service to integrate with Key Vault, either using a Managed Identity to fetch secrets or using the Key Vault references feature in Azure App Service configuration. The actual secret values are never in plain text in application settings or code.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use a Managed Identity for the App Service to access Key Vault - this eliminates the need to use any credentials even for Key Vault access.
  • Key Vault provides secret rotation and integration - update secrets in Key Vault once without redeploying the app.
  • Key Vault secrets are encrypted with HSMs and only accessible to authorized identities.

questions.title: Accessing Azure Resources Without Credentials
questions.scenario: A new Azure Function app needs to read from an Azure Storage account and write to an Azure Cosmos DB, but you want no hard-coded keys or passwords in your function code or configuration.
questions.questionText: What Azure feature can you use to give the function app authenticated access to these resources?

choices.text: Store connection strings in app settings

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What Azure feature gives a resource its own identity in Azure AD so it can authenticate to other services without storing any credentials?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Enable a Managed Identity on the Azure Function and use Azure AD-based access control for the other resources. With a managed identity, the function gets an identity in Azure AD automatically. Assign this identity appropriate access roles (e.g., Storage Blob Data Reader/Writer, Cosmos DB Data Contributor). Inside the function code, use Azure SDKs that leverage the Managed Identity to obtain OAuth tokens silently.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The function can request a token by calling the local Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) endpoint - no human or code ever sees a password.
  • Microsoft takes care of rotating the underlying credentials of the identity, eliminating secret management overhead.
  • Managed identities can be system-assigned (one per resource) or user-assigned (a standalone identity attached to many resources).

questions.title: User Authentication for a Web Application
questions.scenario: You are building a multi-tier web application with a frontend SPA and backend API hosted on Azure. Only employees from your organization should access this app. You want to implement single sign-on using Microsoft 365 identities.
questions.questionText: What is the recommended approach to authenticate users and secure the API on Azure?

choices.text: Use API keys for each user
Use Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) with OAuth/OIDC

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Employees already have Microsoft 365 identities. Which identity platform lets you leverage those existing accounts for SSO with standard protocols?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Leverage the Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) identity platform for both user sign-in and securing the API. Register apps in Entra ID for front-end and back-end. The SPA uses OAuth 2.0/OIDC flow to sign in users with organizational credentials. Upon success, the front-end receives ID and access tokens. The backend API validates JWT bearer tokens to ensure only authorized calls are allowed.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure AD supports Role-Based Access Control through app roles or groups in tokens - the API can check token claims for roles.
  • Enable advanced security like Conditional Access and MFA without changing the app - configured in Azure AD.
  • For SPAs, use authorization code flow with PKCE (which MSAL.js supports) rather than implicit flow.

questions.title: Exposing APIs to Partners Securely
questions.scenario: Your company has internal REST APIs running on Azure App Service and Azure Functions that will be consumed by external business partners. Requirements include rate limiting, API key validation, and a developer portal for partner onboarding.
questions.questionText: What Azure service should you put in front of these APIs?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: You need rate limiting, API key validation, and a developer portal in one layer. What kind of service sits between consumers and backend APIs to provide these cross-cutting concerns?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Introduce Azure API Management to publish and manage the APIs. API Management acts as a secure API gateway between your backend services and consumers. With APIM, you can secure APIs with subscription keys or JWT tokens, apply rate limiting and quotas, perform transformations, and provide a built-in developer portal for partner onboarding.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• APIM policies let you check for valid OAuth tokens, rewrite URLs, add caching, and set quotas - all without changing application code.
  • APIM can integrate with Azure AD B2B/B2C or other IdPs for partner identities.
  • It's multi-region capable in Premium tier for global performance and supports mTLS certificate authentication.

questions.title: Monitoring and Diagnostics
questions.scenario: An Azure-based inventory application is experiencing intermittent slowdowns and errors in production. The development team needs to collect insights into request execution times, failure rates, and trace logs to identify bottlenecks.
questions.questionText: What Azure service should you use to instrument and monitor the application?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: You need an APM tool that captures request timing, failure rates, and trace logs with minimal code changes. Which Azure Monitor feature is purpose-built for this?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use Azure Monitor Application Insights to instrument and monitor the app. Application Insights is a developer-focused APM service that automatically collects telemetry: HTTP request durations, response codes, exceptions, dependency calls, and custom events. It provides Application Map, Failures view, Performance analysis, and the ability to query logs using Log Analytics.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Application Insights can do distributed tracing across services - track a transaction across components and see where time is spent.
  • Smart detection and anomaly analysis automatically detect anomalies in usage or performance and notify you.
  • It integrates with Visual Studio and can be used during local debugging with the SDK to see live metrics.

questions.title: Improving Read Performance with Caching
questions.scenario: A news website hosted on Azure App Service is experiencing high load on its database because each page request fetches the latest headlines. Headlines change only every few minutes.
questions.questionText: How can you improve performance and reduce database load?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Headlines change only every few minutes but are read on every request. What architectural layer sits between the app and database to serve repeated reads from memory?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Implement a caching layer using Azure Cache for Redis to store the news headlines. Load headlines from the database once, store them in Redis (an in-memory data store), and have the web app read from cache on subsequent requests. Azure Cache for Redis responds in sub-millisecond times. Use a cache-aside pattern with TTL for periodic refresh.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Choose an eviction policy and expiration - time-based expiration or use pub/sub for cache invalidation when new headlines are published.
  • Handle cache failures gracefully - if Redis is unavailable, fallback to DB reads.
  • Redis is a distributed cache - multiple app server instances share the same cache and get consistent data.

questions.title: Zero-Downtime Deployment
questions.scenario: You have an Azure App Service hosting a critical web API. Updates are deployed weekly. You want to avoid any downtime during deployments and test a new release in production environment before switching traffic.
questions.questionText: What App Service feature should you use?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can you deploy and test a new version in a production-like environment, then switch traffic atomically with zero downtime?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure App Service Deployment Slots allow parallel deployments (staging and production). Deploy the new API version to the staging slot while production continues serving the old version. Test in staging, then perform a Swap - this exchanges the environments atomically with near-zero downtime. If issues arise, swap back quickly for rollback.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• When you swap, Azure swaps the Virtual IP addresses of the two slots - traffic doesn't hit the new slot until it's warmed up.
  • You can specify certain settings as "slot sticky" that shouldn't swap between environments.
  • For canary releases, use the traffic redirection feature to direct a small percentage of traffic to the new slot first.

questions.title: Selecting a Messaging Pattern (Queue vs Topic)
questions.scenario: An order processing system must send order events to multiple downstream systems: billing, shipping, analytics, and customer notifications. Each system must receive every order event but process it independently.
questions.questionText: Which Azure messaging service and pattern should you use?

choices.text: Azure Service Bus Topic with Subscriptions

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Multiple independent consumers each need a copy of every message. Which messaging pattern supports this fan-out delivery model?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Publish order events to a Service Bus Topic and create one Subscription per consumer (billing/shipping/analytics/notifications). Each subscription gets a copy of every message (fan-out), consumers can scale independently, and the producer stays decoupled from consumer count. Use filters/rules if some consumers only need subsets.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Service Bus topics support subscription rules (SQL filters/correlation) to route subsets without changing publishers.
  • DLQ is per subscription, isolating failures.
  • For strict ordering per key, use Sessions with SessionId (e.g., OrderId). Design consumers as idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.

questions.title: Handling Duplicate Messages
questions.scenario: A backend service consumes messages from an Azure Service Bus queue. Due to retries and transient failures, the same message may occasionally be delivered more than once. Financial transactions are involved.
questions.questionText: What techniques should be used to ensure idempotent processing?

choices.text: Ignore the issue and process all messages
Make processing idempotent and enable duplicate detection

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: With at-least-once delivery, duplicates are inevitable. What two complementary strategies — one broker-side, one application-side — address this?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Ensure idempotency by storing a processed-message marker keyed by MessageId (or business key like OrderId) in a durable store and skipping repeats. Also enable Service Bus Duplicate Detection (set MessageId consistently and configure the detection window) to drop duplicates at the broker. Use transactions where applicable.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Duplicate detection is time-window-based and depends on stable MessageId; it complements but does not replace idempotent handlers.
  • Use an outbox pattern at the producer to prevent duplicates when DB+publish isn't atomic.
  • Treat 'exactly once' as 'effectively once' via idempotency + dedupe.

questions.title: Choosing Between Event Grid and Service Bus
questions.scenario: You need to notify several internal systems when a user profile is updated. Notifications must be delivered quickly, but if a consumer is temporarily offline, the update should still be processed later.
questions.questionText: Compare Azure Event Grid and Azure Service Bus for this use case - which is better?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: One service is push-based and optimized for instant reaction; the other durably buffers messages for consumers that may be offline. Which model fits better here?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use Service Bus if you need durable, pull-based processing with back-pressure, retries, DLQ, and consumer independence when subscribers are offline. Event Grid is best for lightweight event notifications with fast push delivery, but is less suited for consumers that need durable queues and deferred processing.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Event Grid is an event router with retries/DLQ, not a full message broker - it's optimized for 'react now'.
  • Service Bus adds lock renewal, sessions, and transactions for reliable processing.
  • If ordering per user matters, sessions fit naturally. For massive streams, Event Hubs is the correct primitive.

questions.title: Function Execution Model
questions.scenario: A function processes files uploaded to Blob Storage. Some files are large and processing can take several minutes.
questions.questionText: What considerations must you make regarding Azure Functions execution limits, and which hosting plan should you choose?

choices.text: Premium plan or Dedicated plan for longer execution
Process files synchronously in App Service

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The default serverless plan has a short execution timeout. What happens when processing exceeds it, and which hosting tier removes that constraint?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The Consumption plan has a default timeout of 5 minutes (configurable up to 10 minutes). For functions that process large files taking several minutes, use the Premium plan (which allows longer timeouts up to unbounded with configuration) or a Dedicated (App Service) plan. Premium also provides pre-warmed instances to avoid cold starts.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Premium plan supports VNET integration, larger instance sizes, and no cold start due to always-warm instances.
  • For truly long-running work, consider Durable Functions which checkpoint progress.
  • Monitor execution time and consider breaking work into smaller chunks if possible.

questions.title: Scaling Azure Functions
questions.scenario: An HTTP-triggered Azure Function experiences sudden spikes in traffic during business hours.
questions.questionText: How does Azure Functions automatically scale on the Consumption plan, and what factors influence the number of instances?

choices.text: Automatic scale-out based on incoming event rate and queue length
Scale based on time of day only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about what triggers the platform to add or remove function instances. Is it manual, time-based, or driven by incoming workload signals?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure Functions on Consumption plan uses a scale controller that monitors the rate of events and determines when to add or remove instances. For HTTP triggers, it scales based on request rate. For queue triggers, it considers queue length and message age. Scale-out is automatic and can happen rapidly during traffic spikes.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The scale controller is trigger-specific - each trigger type has its own scaling logic.
  • There's a maximum instance limit (default 200 for Consumption, configurable).
  • Cold starts can occur when scaling out; Premium plan mitigates this with pre-warmed instances.

questions.title: Cold Start Mitigation
questions.scenario: Users report that the first request to a serverless API is sometimes slow after periods of inactivity.
questions.questionText: What causes this behavior in Azure Functions, and what options can mitigate it?

choices.text: Cold start - use Premium plan with always-ready instances

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Why would the very first request after idle time be slow in a serverless model? Think about what happens when no instance is running to handle it.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cold start occurs when Azure needs to allocate a new instance for your function after it has scaled to zero (Consumption plan) or when scaling out. The Premium plan offers pre-warmed instances that are always ready to receive requests. Alternative mitigations include keeping functions warm with scheduled pings or using Dedicated (App Service) plan.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cold start duration depends on runtime, dependencies, and initialization code - minimize startup work.
  • Premium plan allows configuring minimum instances that stay warm.
  • Consider using Azure App Service for latency-sensitive HTTP APIs if cold starts are unacceptable.

questions.title: Securing Outbound API Calls
questions.scenario: Your Azure Function must call an external SaaS API that requires OAuth 2.0 client credentials.
questions.questionText: Where should the client secret be stored, and how should it be accessed securely at runtime?

choices.text: In Azure Key Vault, retrieved at runtime
In the function code as a constant

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Where should secrets live so they never appear in code or config files, and how can the function authenticate to that store without credentials of its own?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Store OAuth client credentials in Azure Key Vault. Enable Managed Identity on the Function App and grant it access to read secrets from Key Vault. At runtime, use Key Vault SDK or Key Vault references in app settings to retrieve the secret. This keeps secrets out of source control and provides audit trails.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Key Vault references allow you to reference a Key Vault secret directly in app settings - the platform resolves it at startup.
  • Cache retrieved secrets in memory to avoid hitting Key Vault on every request (respect rate limits).
  • Use separate Key Vaults for different environments (dev/staging/prod).

questions.title: API Versioning Strategy
questions.scenario: You are exposing a REST API through Azure API Management. Existing clients must continue working while new clients adopt breaking changes.
questions.questionText: What versioning strategies are supported by APIM?

choices.text: URL path, query string, and header-based versioning

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider where version information can travel in an HTTP request: the URL path, query parameters, or headers. How many of these does APIM support?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: APIM natively supports API versioning through URL path segment (/api/v1/resource), query string parameter (?api-version=2024-01-01), or custom HTTP header (api-version: 1.0). You can run multiple versions simultaneously, with each version potentially routing to different backend implementations. Recommend URL path versioning for clarity.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use API revisions for non-breaking changes within a version; use versions for breaking changes.
  • Configure deprecation policies to warn clients when using old versions.
  • Version sets in APIM group related API versions together for management.

questions.title: Protecting APIs from Abuse
questions.scenario: An externally exposed API is experiencing excessive traffic from a small number of consumers, impacting overall performance.
questions.questionText: How can Azure API Management be configured to protect the backend services?

choices.text: Apply rate limiting and throttling policies in APIM

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: A few consumers are using disproportionate capacity. What gateway-level mechanism can cap usage per caller without changing backend code?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use APIM policies like rate-limit-by-key and quota-by-key to limit requests per consumer (by subscription key, JWT claim, or IP address). Configure different limits for different subscription tiers. APIM returns 429 Too Many Requests when limits are exceeded, protecting backends without code changes.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Rate limits are typically short-term (requests per second), quotas are longer-term (calls per month).
  • Use the rate-limit-by-key policy with expressions to identify callers by custom attributes.
  • Combine with caching policies to reduce backend load for frequently requested data.

questions.title: Retry and Transient Fault Handling
questions.scenario: A web app hosted on Azure App Service occasionally fails when calling a downstream Azure SQL Database due to transient connectivity issues.
questions.questionText: How should the application be designed to handle these failures gracefully?

choices.text: Fail immediately and show error to user
Implement retry logic with exponential backoff

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Transient failures are temporary by nature. What resilience pattern automatically re-attempts failed calls with increasing wait times?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use retry logic with exponential backoff for transient failures. Azure SDKs and libraries like Polly (.NET) provide built-in retry mechanisms. Azure SQL supports Connection Retry through SqlClient configuration. Implement the pattern: detect transient errors, wait with exponential delay, retry up to a maximum count, then fail gracefully.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SqlClient has built-in connection resiliency - enable ConnectRetryCount and ConnectRetryInterval in connection string.
  • Use circuit breaker pattern for repeated failures to avoid overwhelming a degraded service.
  • Log retries for monitoring and set alerts on retry rates.

questions.title: Designing for High Availability
questions.scenario: A mission-critical web API must remain available even if a single Azure region experiences an outage.
questions.questionText: What Azure deployment strategies should be used to achieve regional resilience?

choices.text: Multi-region deployment with global load balancing

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: If a single region can fail, what deployment topology ensures the API survives that failure? Think about redundancy across fault domains.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Deploy the API to multiple Azure regions and use Azure Front Door or Traffic Manager for global load balancing and automatic failover. Configure health probes to detect regional failures. Use geo-replicated data stores (Cosmos DB multi-region, Azure SQL geo-replication) to ensure data availability across regions.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure Front Door provides global HTTP load balancing with sub-second failover and WAF capabilities.
  • Consider active-active vs active-passive patterns based on consistency requirements.
  • Test failover scenarios regularly and monitor RTO/RPO metrics.

questions.title: Load Balancing HTTP Traffic
questions.scenario: You deploy the same web application to two different Azure regions. Users are distributed globally.
questions.questionText: What Azure service should be used to route user requests to the closest healthy region?

choices.text: Azure Front Door or Traffic Manager

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Users are global and the app runs in two regions. You need a service that routes each user to the nearest healthy backend. Is that a regional or global load balancer?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure Front Door provides global HTTP load balancing with anycast routing to the closest POP, then routes to the healthiest backend. Traffic Manager uses DNS-based routing with performance, priority, or weighted methods. Both support health probes for automatic failover. Front Door is preferred for HTTP workloads due to its edge features.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Front Door operates at Layer 7 with features like URL rewriting, SSL offload, and WAF.
  • Traffic Manager operates at DNS level and works with any protocol.
  • Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway are regional services, not global.

questions.title: Configuring Application Settings
questions.scenario: An application requires different configuration values for development, staging, and production environments.
questions.questionText: How should these values be managed in Azure to avoid code changes between environments?

choices.text: Use Azure App Service Application Settings and deployment slots
Use configuration files committed to source control
Use different code branches per environment

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can you inject different configuration values per environment at runtime without changing the deployed code? Think about platform-level settings and slot isolation.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Configure application settings in Azure App Service (or Function App) for each environment. These settings become environment variables at runtime. Use deployment slots for staging with slot-specific (sticky) settings that don't swap with code. This separates configuration from code and allows the same deployment package across environments.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• For complex configuration, use Azure App Configuration service with feature flags and dynamic refresh.
  • Store secrets in Key Vault and reference them in app settings using Key Vault references.
  • CI/CD pipelines can deploy configuration alongside code using ARM templates or Bicep.

questions.title: Feature Flag Management
questions.scenario: You want to enable or disable application features at runtime without redeploying the application. Gradual rollout is required.
questions.questionText: Which Azure service supports this pattern?

choices.text: Azure App Configuration with Feature Flags

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: You need runtime feature toggling with gradual rollout — not a redeploy. Which Azure service provides centralized feature flag management with targeting filters?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure App Configuration's Feature Manager supports feature flags with targeting filters (percentage rollout, user groups, time windows). Applications integrate via SDK to check feature state at runtime. Changes take effect without redeployment. Combine with A/B testing and user targeting for controlled releases.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Feature filters enable complex targeting: percentage-based, time-window, targeting specific users/groups.
  • SDK supports dynamic refresh - app can poll or use push notifications for flag changes.
  • Integrate with Application Insights for feature-specific telemetry and impact analysis.

questions.title: Storing Application Logs
questions.scenario: An Azure Function generates structured logs that need to be retained for compliance and queried later for investigations.
questions.questionText: Where should these logs be stored, and how can they be queried efficiently?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Structured logs need long-term retention and ad-hoc querying. Which Azure Monitor component stores logs and supports a rich query language?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Configure Azure Functions to send logs to a Log Analytics workspace (via Application Insights or directly). Log Analytics provides long-term retention (configurable), powerful querying with KQL, alerts, and dashboards. For compliance, set appropriate retention periods and export to storage if needed for archival.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use ILogger in your function code for structured logging - properties become queryable fields.
  • Set up log-based alerts for critical patterns (errors, security events).
  • Export logs to Azure Storage or Event Hubs for long-term archival beyond Log Analytics retention limits.

questions.title: Distributed Tracing Across Services
questions.scenario: A request flows through an Azure App Service, an Azure Function, and a downstream API. You need to trace a single request end-to-end.
questions.questionText: How can you trace a single request across these components?

choices.text: Application Insights distributed tracing with correlation
Manual correlation IDs in each service

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can correlation IDs be automatically propagated across HTTP boundaries so you see one end-to-end timeline for a single request?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Configure all services to use the same Application Insights resource (or connect multiple instances). Application Insights automatically propagates correlation IDs (operation_Id, parent_Id) in HTTP headers across service calls. The Application Map and End-to-End Transaction views show the complete request flow with timing at each hop.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use W3C Trace Context headers for cross-service correlation - supported by default in modern SDKs.
  • Custom telemetry can be added with TelemetryClient to enrich traces with business context.
  • Enable sampling carefully to balance data volume with trace completeness for debugging.

questions.title: Asynchronous vs Synchronous APIs
questions.scenario: A long-running background operation is currently implemented as a synchronous HTTP API call, causing timeouts for clients.
questions.questionText: How should the API be redesigned using Azure services to improve reliability?

choices.text: Use async request-reply pattern with queues and status polling

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: A synchronous call that takes minutes will time out. What pattern lets the API accept work immediately and handle processing in the background?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Redesign to async pattern: API accepts request and immediately returns HTTP 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to a status endpoint. Enqueue work to Azure Service Bus or Storage Queue. Background worker (Function or WebJob) processes the job. Client polls the status endpoint or registers a webhook callback for completion notification.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Durable Functions provide built-in HTTP async pattern with status query endpoints.
  • Consider Azure SignalR for real-time push notifications instead of polling.
  • Store job status in durable storage (Table Storage, Cosmos DB) for reliability across worker restarts.

questions.title: Designing a Callback Pattern
questions.scenario: An external system submits jobs to your API and needs to be notified when processing completes.
questions.questionText: What Azure-native approach can be used to implement callbacks securely and reliably?

choices.text: Webhooks with Azure Event Grid or Service Bus

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Instead of the client polling for completion, how can the system push a notification to the client's endpoint when the job finishes?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Implement webhook callbacks: clients register their callback URL when submitting jobs. On completion, publish an event to Azure Event Grid which delivers to the webhook endpoint with retry logic. Alternatively, use Azure Logic Apps or direct HTTP calls with Polly for retry. Validate callback URLs and use secrets/signatures for security.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Event Grid validates webhook endpoints during subscription using validation handshake.
  • Use CloudEvents schema for interoperability.
  • Implement dead-letter handling for failed deliveries and notify operators.

questions.title: Using Durable Timers
questions.scenario: A workflow requires waiting exactly 24 hours before executing a follow-up action, even if the app restarts.
questions.questionText: How can this be implemented in a serverless, reliable way?

choices.text: Timer trigger with state in memory

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The timer must survive app restarts and consume no resources while waiting. Which serverless extension supports durable, checkpoint-backed timers?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Durable Functions provides CreateTimer API in orchestrator functions. The timer is durable - the orchestrator checkpoints its state and resumes after the timer fires, even if the function app restarts. The orchestrator consumes no resources while waiting. Combine with external events for timeout patterns.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Durable timers use Azure Storage for state - they survive restarts and scale events.
  • Timers can be canceled using CancellationToken for timeout patterns.
  • For recurring schedules, use timer triggers; for workflow waits, use durable timers.

questions.title: Handling Poison Messages
questions.scenario: A message repeatedly fails processing and is retried multiple times in Azure Service Bus.
questions.questionText: How does Azure Service Bus handle such messages, and how should your application respond?

choices.text: Messages are moved to dead-letter queue (DLQ) after max delivery attempts
Messages are deleted after first failure

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What happens to a message that has been retried beyond the configured maximum? Where does the broker park it for inspection?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Service Bus moves messages to the dead-letter queue after exceeding MaxDeliveryCount (default 10). Your application should: set appropriate MaxDeliveryCount, monitor DLQ depth with alerts, and implement a DLQ processor to inspect, fix, and resubmit or archive failed messages. Dead-lettered messages include reason codes for diagnosis.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• DLQ messages include DeadLetterReason and DeadLetterErrorDescription properties.
  • DLQ has its own entity path: queue/$deadletterqueue or topic/subscription/$deadletterqueue.
  • Set up alerts on DLQ message count and implement automated or manual remediation workflows.

questions.title: Database Connection Management
questions.scenario: An App Service scales out under load, but database connections are exhausted.
questions.questionText: What design practices should be applied to prevent this issue?

choices.text: Create new connection for each request
Use connection pooling and limit pool size

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: When many app instances each open fresh connections, the database runs out. What technique reuses existing connections instead of creating new ones?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use connection pooling (built into ADO.NET by default) and configure Max Pool Size appropriately across all instances. Ensure using statements or proper disposal return connections to pool. Consider Azure SQL elastic pools for workload variability. Monitor connection usage and set alerts.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Calculate max connections = (App Service instances) × (Pool size per instance) and ensure DB can handle it.
  • Use async database operations to avoid blocking connections during I/O wait.
  • Consider adding a caching layer (Redis) to reduce database load and connection pressure.

questions.title: Choosing Storage Tiers
questions.scenario: A Blob Storage account contains frequently accessed images, infrequently accessed reports, and long-term archives.
questions.questionText: How should storage tiers be selected to minimize cost?

choices.text: Use Hot for images, Cool for reports, Archive for archives

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Each access pattern has a different cost tradeoff between storage price and retrieval price. How should you match tiers to frequency of access?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Match access patterns to tiers: Hot (lowest access cost, higher storage cost), Cool (lower storage cost, higher access cost, 30-day minimum), Archive (lowest storage cost, highest retrieval cost, hours to rehydrate). Use lifecycle management rules to automatically move blobs between tiers based on age or last access time.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Archive tier requires rehydration (Standard: 15 hours, High-priority: 1 hour) before reading.
  • Lifecycle rules can transition or delete blobs automatically based on filters (prefix, blob type, age).
  • Enable access time tracking for more granular lifecycle decisions (requires additional cost).

questions.title: Data Encryption Requirements
questions.scenario: Sensitive customer data is stored in Azure Storage and Azure SQL Database. Regulatory compliance requires encryption.
questions.questionText: What encryption mechanisms does Azure provide by default?

choices.text: Encryption at rest by default; TLS in transit

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Does Azure require you to opt in to encryption, or is data protected by default? Think about both data at rest and data in transit.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure provides encryption at rest by default for Storage (SSE) and SQL Database (TDE) using Microsoft-managed keys. All data in transit uses TLS 1.2+. For additional control, use customer-managed keys (CMK) stored in Key Vault. SQL Database also supports Always Encrypted for sensitive columns.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• CMK with Key Vault gives you control over key rotation and can meet compliance requirements.
  • SQL Always Encrypted protects data even from DBAs - only client with key can decrypt.
  • For defense in depth, combine encryption at rest, in transit, and client-side encryption where needed.

questions.title: Managed Identity Scope
questions.scenario: A single managed identity is used by multiple applications to access Azure resources.
questions.questionText: What are the tradeoffs between using a system-assigned versus a user-assigned managed identity in this scenario?

choices.text: User-assigned is better for sharing across multiple resources; system-assigned is tied to one resource

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: One identity type lives and dies with its resource; the other is a standalone object shareable across many resources. Which fits a multi-app scenario better?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: System-assigned identity is created for and tied to a single Azure resource - deleted when the resource is deleted. User-assigned identity is a standalone Azure resource that can be attached to multiple applications. For least privilege, user-assigned allows centralized permission management for a group of apps with similar access needs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• User-assigned identities persist independently - useful for blue-green deployments or resource recreation.
  • A resource can have both system-assigned and multiple user-assigned identities.
  • For single-use resources, system-assigned is simpler; for shared access patterns, user-assigned provides better management.

questions.title: Securing Storage Access
questions.scenario: An application must allow read-only access to certain blobs for anonymous users, while keeping other blobs private.
questions.questionText: How can this be achieved securely in Azure Blob Storage?

choices.text: Use container-level access policies or SAS for specific blobs

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Some blobs need anonymous read access while others must stay private. How can you separate these access levels at the container or individual blob level?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Create separate containers: one with public read access (container or blob level), another private. Alternatively, keep all containers private and generate short-lived SAS tokens for blobs that need temporary public access. For CDN scenarios, use Azure CDN with private origin and token authentication.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Container public access can be disabled at the storage account level for compliance.
  • Use stored access policies with SAS for centralized revocation capability.
  • Azure CDN with private link origin provides caching without exposing storage directly.

questions.title: Choosing Between Logic Apps and Functions
questions.scenario: A business workflow integrates multiple SaaS systems, requires visual monitoring, and includes conditional logic and retries.
questions.questionText: Should you use Azure Logic Apps or Azure Functions?

choices.text: Azure Logic Apps for visual workflow with connectors

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The workflow is integration-heavy with many SaaS connectors and needs visual monitoring. Is this better suited for code-first or declarative-visual orchestration?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Logic Apps excels at integration workflows: 400+ built-in connectors for SaaS/enterprise systems, visual designer, built-in retry and error handling, run history for monitoring. Use Functions when you need custom code, high-performance compute, or granular control. Logic Apps can call Functions for complex processing steps.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Logic Apps Standard offers single-tenant deployment with VS Code development experience.
  • Non-developers can view and understand Logic Apps workflows through the visual designer.
  • Logic Apps pricing is per action execution; Functions is per execution + GB-seconds - compare for your workload.

questions.title: Handling Configuration Refresh
questions.scenario: Configuration values stored centrally are updated while the application is running. The application needs to pick up changes without restarting.
questions.questionText: How can the application pick up configuration changes dynamically?

choices.text: Use Azure App Configuration with dynamic refresh

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The app needs to detect configuration changes without restarting. What centralized config service supports live refresh via polling or push?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure App Configuration SDK supports dynamic refresh: configure a sentinel key that triggers refresh when changed, or use Event Grid integration for push-based refresh. The application polls App Configuration periodically and updates configuration without restart. Use caching intervals to balance freshness with performance.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use a sentinel key pattern: change one key to signal all clients to refresh their full configuration.
  • Event Grid integration enables near real-time push updates instead of polling.
  • Combine with IOptionsSnapshot or IOptionsMonitor patterns in .NET for automatic config refresh.

questions.title: Designing for Cost Optimization
questions.scenario: An Azure Function processes messages sporadically, with long idle periods.
questions.questionText: Which hosting plan minimizes cost?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Long idle periods mean you're paying for nothing if the plan charges for always-on capacity. Which hosting model charges only when code actually runs?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Consumption plan charges only for actual executions (per GB-second and execution count). During idle periods, no charges accrue. Premium and Dedicated plans charge for always-on capacity. Tradeoff: Consumption has cold starts and timeout limits, which may not suit all workloads.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Consumption plan includes a free grant: 400,000 GB-s and 1 million executions per month.
  • For unpredictable but latency-sensitive loads, Premium with minimum instances may balance cost/performance.
  • Monitor execution patterns to validate the right plan choice over time.

questions.title: Throttling Downstream Dependencies
questions.scenario: A backend API depends on a third-party service with strict rate limits.
questions.questionText: How can Azure services help prevent exceeding those limits?

choices.text: Use queues with controlled consumption rate and circuit breaker patterns
Make unlimited calls and handle errors

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can you decouple request arrival rate from the rate at which you call the downstream service, and what pattern stops calls when the service is overwhelmed?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Queue requests to Azure Service Bus/Storage Queue and process at controlled rate using maxConcurrentCalls or manual throttling. Implement circuit breaker (via Polly or similar) to back off when rate limit errors occur. Cache responses where possible to reduce API calls. Use APIM policies for outbound rate limiting.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Parse rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After) to adaptively throttle.
  • Use token bucket or leaky bucket algorithm for smooth rate limiting.
  • Consider request coalescing or batching where the API supports it.

questions.title: Implementing Health Checks
questions.scenario: A load balancer must know whether an application instance is healthy before routing traffic to it.
questions.questionText: How are health checks implemented in Azure App Service?

choices.text: Configure Health Check path in App Service settings

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The load balancer needs a way to know if an instance is healthy. What endpoint-based mechanism does App Service provide for this probing?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Enable Health Check in App Service configuration, specifying a path to your health endpoint. Azure probes this endpoint periodically; if it fails multiple times, the instance is removed from load balancer and optionally replaced. Your /health endpoint should check critical dependencies (database, external services) and return appropriate HTTP status.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Health check endpoint should be fast, lightweight, and test real dependencies.
  • Return 200 for healthy, 500+ for unhealthy. Consider liveness vs readiness semantics.
  • Combine with Application Insights availability tests for external monitoring.

questions.title: Secure File Processing Pipeline
questions.scenario: Uploaded files must be virus-scanned before being made available for download.
questions.questionText: How can this be implemented using Azure services in an event-driven manner?

choices.text: Event Grid triggers function to scan, move clean files to approved container

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about a two-stage container pattern: files land in one container, get scanned event-driven, and only move to a second container if clean.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Pattern: Upload files to a quarantine/incoming container. Event Grid triggers Azure Function on blob creation. Function calls Microsoft Defender for Storage API or third-party antivirus. Clean files are moved to an approved container; infected files are deleted or quarantined. Only the approved container is accessible for downloads.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Microsoft Defender for Storage provides built-in malware scanning with events published to Event Grid.
  • For custom scanning, use ClamAV in a container or third-party APIs.
  • Implement dead-letter handling for scan failures and alert on suspicious activity patterns.

questions.title: Designing for Observability
questions.scenario: Beyond logging errors, you need to understand application behavior under load.
questions.questionText: What additional telemetry should be collected?

choices.text: Metrics, traces, custom events, and dependency tracking

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Beyond error logs, think about the three pillars of observability. What additional signal types give you a complete picture of application behavior?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Full observability requires: Metrics (RED: Rate, Errors, Duration), distributed traces showing request flow across services, logs with structured context, custom events for business milestones, and dependency tracking for external calls. Use Application Insights for unified collection and correlation.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Follow the three pillars of observability: metrics, logs, and traces.
  • Add custom dimensions to telemetry for business context (tenant ID, feature flag state, etc.).
  • Create dashboards combining technical and business metrics for holistic visibility.

questions.title: Choosing Between SQL and NoSQL
questions.scenario: An application stores both transactional order data and large volumes of semi-structured event data.
questions.questionText: How should data storage be split across Azure services?

choices.text: Use Azure SQL for orders, Cosmos DB or Table Storage for events

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Transactional data needs ACID and relational integrity; event data needs flexible schema and high throughput. Should both live in the same store?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Match storage to access patterns: Azure SQL for relational order data with transactions, referential integrity, and complex queries. Cosmos DB for globally distributed, high-throughput event data with flexible schema. Table Storage for simpler, cost-effective event storage if global distribution isn't needed. Consider Event Hubs for ingestion before storage.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Polyglot persistence: use the right database for each workload.
  • For analytics on events, consider landing in Data Lake Storage and querying with Synapse.
  • Use change data capture (CDC) or events to keep systems synchronized if needed.

questions.title: Graceful Shutdown Handling
questions.scenario: An App Service instance is being scaled down while processing requests. You need to ensure in-flight work is completed.
questions.questionText: How should the application be designed to shut down gracefully?

choices.text: Handle application stopping events and complete in-flight work

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: When the platform signals shutdown, the app has a grace period. What should it do during that window to avoid dropping in-flight work?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Implement graceful shutdown: listen for shutdown signals (SIGTERM, IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping), stop accepting new requests, complete in-flight operations, and flush any buffered data. App Service provides a configurable shutdown timeout (default 90 seconds for Windows). For long-running operations, consider checkpointing progress to resume elsewhere.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use CancellationToken propagation to signal in-flight operations to complete quickly.
  • For message processing, don't complete/delete messages until processing is truly done.
  • Consider using Durable Functions for long-running work that can checkpoint and resume on any instance.

term-durable-functions.name: Durable Functions
term-durable-functions.definition: Azure Functions extension enabling stateful orchestrations with automatic checkpointing and replay.
term-durable-functions.examNote: Use for multi-step workflows, fan-out/fan-in, and human interaction patterns.

term-cosmos-db.name: Azure Cosmos DB
term-cosmos-db.definition: Globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database with tunable consistency and automatic scaling.
term-cosmos-db.examNote: Best for global distribution, flexible schema, and low-latency requirements.

term-event-grid.name: Azure Event Grid
term-event-grid.definition: Fully managed event routing service for reactive, event-driven architectures.
term-event-grid.examNote: Use for Azure service events and lightweight push notifications, not for durable queuing.

term-event-hubs.name: Azure Event Hubs
term-event-hubs.definition: Big data streaming platform for high-throughput event ingestion (millions of events/second).
term-event-hubs.examNote: Use for telemetry, IoT data ingestion, and stream processing scenarios.

term-service-bus.name: Azure Service Bus
term-service-bus.definition: Enterprise message broker with queues and topics supporting transactions, sessions, and dead-lettering.
term-service-bus.examNote: Use for reliable messaging, ordering, and enterprise integration patterns.

term-apim.name: Azure API Management
term-apim.definition: API gateway service for publishing, securing, and managing APIs with policies and developer portal.
term-apim.examNote: Use for rate limiting, authentication, versioning, and partner API exposure.

term-app-insights.name: Application Insights
term-app-insights.definition: APM service for monitoring live applications with automatic telemetry collection and distributed tracing.
term-app-insights.examNote: Enable for request tracking, dependency monitoring, and performance diagnostics.

term-managed-identity.name: Managed Identity
term-managed-identity.definition: Azure AD identity automatically managed for Azure resources, eliminating credential management.
term-managed-identity.examNote: Prefer managed identity over connection strings for Azure-to-Azure authentication.

term-key-vault.name: Azure Key Vault
term-key-vault.definition: Secure secret, key, and certificate management service with HSM backing and access control.
term-key-vault.examNote: Store all secrets here, access via managed identity and Key Vault references.

term-deployment-slots.name: Deployment Slots
term-deployment-slots.definition: App Service feature enabling blue-green deployments with zero-downtime swaps.
term-deployment-slots.examNote: Use for staging, testing in production environment, and instant rollback.
